REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX (the claimant) is a citizen of the People's Republic of China. The claimant claims to have well-founded fear of persecution at the hands of the Communist regime and in particular, the Public Security Bureau, by reason of his religion as a Christian under sections 96 and 97 of The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1
ALLEGATIONS

[2] The claimant alleges in his Personal Information Form2 that as a result of his wife having been forced to have an abortion, he became sad and despondent, he turned to an underground Christian church on the recommendation of a friend. The claimant maintains that he started to attend the underground Christian church in XXXX 2009. The claimant indicated that he attended regularly on Sundays. The claimant indicated that on XXXX XXXX, 2011, his underground Christian church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (the PSB). The claimant indicated that he was able to escape and went to the home of a relative. The claimant alleges that the PSB went to his home to arrest him for his underground Christian church activities. The claimant stated that arrangements were made with a snakehead (smuggler) to leave the country. The claimant came to Canada on or about XXXX XXXX, 2011, and claimed for refugee protection several days later.
DETERMINATION

[3] I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. I find that the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that on the balance of probabilities he would personally be subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to the People's Republic of China.
ANALYSIS
Identity

subthemes.text:
[4] The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documents filed3 establish his identity as a citizen of the People's Republic of China.
The claimant as a Member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China

[5] I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant stated that he went to the underground church every week and the second time he went to it (i.e. in XXXX 2009), he was given a Bible. The claimant was asked what he did at the underground church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant responded that there was a Bible reading. The claimant was asked if there was anything else. The claimant then said that the members would share their faith and when asked as to what that meant, he responded that members shared what they had learned from the Bible. When asked for a third time if there was anything else the claimant did at his underground Christian church, he indicated that members gave a donation and helped distribute flyers. The claimant was asked for a fourth time if there was anything else he did at his underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant responded that if a member faced hardship, then the other members would assist that person. The claimant was asked if praying was done at the underground church, to which he replied in the affirmative. When asked as to why he failed to mention prayers, the claimant stated that he was sorry and was nervous. I reject this explanation as prayers are a central aspect to any Christian church.

[6] The claimant was asked about the alleged raid by the PSB on his underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant indicated that when advised by the leader that the PSB were approaching, he ran out the back door. The claimant stated that he had to go across a frozen ditch, up a mountain with fruit trees to get to a public road. The claimant acknowledged that the PSB are the professional police force in the People's Republic of China. The claimant was asked if the PSB were going to raid this underground church, would they not have surrounded the building and not simply go to the front door so people could run out the back door. The claimant replied that the PSB could not get to the back door. When asked to explain, the claimant initially stated that there was only one way in and one way out. When asked again, the claimant stated that the road was one way so the PSB could not get to the back door. When asked if the PSB could go on foot to the back door, the claimant answered in the affirmative. The claimant was then asked if the PSB could get to the back door why was the house not surrounded, the claimant replied that the PSB did not know how to come to him and the others. I reject this explanation. If the PSB were going to raid this underground church, they would have surrounded the building and not simply go to the front door so people could run out the back door. Furthermore, the claimant would not have any knowledge as to what the PSB knew or did not know with regard to getting to the back door. The claimant was asked as to what he did upon escaping from the underground church. He replied that he went home. When it was pointed out to him that in his Personal Information Form, he stated that he went to the home of a distant cousin, the claimant then said it was his auntie's home and that his cousin lived there as well but that he always said that it was his home. I reject this explanation as I find that the claimant was simply trying to cover his mistake in his oral testimony.

[7] The claimant, to support his claim that he is wanted by the PSB filed a summons.4 The summons indicates that it is an "Arrest Summons". There is no objective evidence that the PSB issued an "arrest summons" as indicated in the National Documentation Package for China,5 dated October 31, 2017. Furthermore, as indicated in the decision of Huang v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), "overall credibility may affect the weight given to the documentary evidence".6 I am mindful of the presence of fraudulent documents7 from the People's Republic of China and since I have found that the claimant was not a member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China I therefore do not find that the summons proffered by the claimant to be authentic.
Exit from the People's Republic of China

[8] The claimant indicated that a snakehead (smuggler) was hired to assist him in leaving the People's Republic of China. When asked as to how he was able to leave the country if wanted by the PSB, the claimant responded that he did not know and that the smuggler had arranged everything. The claimant indicated that he used his genuine Chinese passport and showed it to a customs officer who stamped it. The claimant was asked if he had to show his passport to any other Chinese official to which he responded in the negative. I reject this explanation as the claimant would have had to have shown his passport to possibly more Chinese customs officials and at least to airline officials prior to boarding the plane.

[9] I have also considered the Chairperson's Jurisprudential Guide TB6-11632.8 I have also considered the opposing case law such as the recent decision in Huang v. MCI9 wherein Russell J. outlined case law and opposing arguments that must be considered when assessing a claimant's ability to leave the People's Republic of China on his or her own genuine passport. Among those arguments stated in the case law are the following key points: (a) That a well-placed bribe to an official with a computer may be sufficient to compromise the Golden Shield system, thereby permitting a claimant to leave the People's Republic of China undetected; and (b) Whereas corruption is endemic in the People's Republic of China, it is plausible for a snakehead (smuggler) may successfully help a claimant bypass the Golden Shield police computer system and authorities. I have reviewed TB6-11632 and find that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) did address and consider this opposing case law and these specific arguments.10 The RAD in TB6-11632 outlined extensive evidence in the national documentation package about exit controls in the People's Republic of China. Many of these exit controls were in place when the claimant left the country. I find that the claimant's description of his flight from the People's Republic of China is not consistent with that as described in the national documentation evidence. The claimant was quite vague with respect as to his ability to leave the People's Republic of China: he indicated that he showed his passport to only one Chinese official and then boarded a plane at the Beijing Airport. When asked as to how he avoided the Golden Shield computer system, the claimant indicated that he did not know. The national documentation evidence describes multiple levels of security checks and instances where passports are screened. I find that the claimant could not have successfully left the People's Republic of China in the manner he has described of showing his passport to one Chinese official who stamped, scanned or examined it and then was able to board a plane.

[10] I have also considered the opposing arguments regarding bribery and endemic corruption in the People's Republic of China. These arguments do not address my concerns in the current case as outlined in the previous paragraph. Where the claimant himself is not credible with respect to his travel through the airport, arguments about bribery and corruption make little difference. I adopt the reasoning of the RAD in TB6-11632. While it is plausible or possible that a wanted fugitive may be smuggled out of the People's Republic of China, I need not accept it or believe it to be probable in the current case. In the current case, given the claimant's lack of credibility about being a member of an underground Christian church, I find it unlikely that he was smuggled out of the country. I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not leave the People's Republic of China as he described using his own genuine Chinese passport. I therefore find that the claimant is not being sought by the Chinese authorities for being a member of an underground Christian church. In conclusion, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China and has never been wanted by Chinese authorities.
The Claimant as a Christian in Canada

[11] I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a Christian in Canada. The claimant had stated that he started to practice Christianity in the People's Republic of China in XXXX 2009 and also received a Bible within a couple of weeks of his first attendance. The claimant stated that he started attending the XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2011, and although he stated he was baptized in the People's Republic of China, was again baptized in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2011, as stated on his Baptism Certificate.11 The claimant stated that he had a Bible in Canada as of early May 2011 and one in the People's Republic of China as of November 2009, and read it in both countries. The claimant has twelve years of formal education. The claimant stated that he went to church here in Canada every week until the last few months because he hurt his back.

[12] The claimant was asked as to what the denomination of the XXXX XXXX XXXX and replied protestant. The claimant was asked again and was given examples such as Anglican, Methodist, and Presbyterian. The claimant indicated that he did not know. The claimant was asked to tell a story from the Old Testament, other than the story of creation. The claimant replied that he was nervous and could not remember. The claimant was asked to name the apostles. The claimant named some of the disciples. The claimant did know the concept of God existing in three persons, could provide limited information about Holy Communion: the cookie is the body of Christ and the grape juice the blood of Christ and did provide a parable from the New Testament. The claimant was asked about his activities at his church here in Canada. The claimant stated that basically he participated in activities at Christmas, Easter and Pentecost. When asked as to what these activities entailed, the claimant indicated that he went to church and prayed. I am mindful that the level of knowledge of one's professed religion is one that can reasonably be expected. The claimant alleges that he has been a Christian since November 2009, a period of over eight years and has been reading the Bible from that time as well. I find that the level of knowledge of Christianity of the claimant is extremely poor. He was not able to tell a story from the Old Testament (other than the story of creation) was not able to name the apostles and was extremely vague as to major religious celebrations such as Christmas and Easter at his church. Moreover, the Certificate of Baptism is from XXXX 2011, his photos12 are from XXXX 2011 and the church letter is dated August 20, 2013,13 indicating that if the claimant was truly a Christian and had been attending church here in Canada over six and a half years, would have more knowledge. Furthermore, when questioned by his counsel as what his religion does for him, the claimant replied that it changed his life and when asked to explain, stated that he feels lots of joy and when asked as to how his faith allows him so much joy, he indicated that after I read the Bible, he felt it. I find, on a balance of probabilities that the previous answers are vague and not from a person who has been a devout Christian for over eight years.

[13] In summary, I find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant, upon his arrival to Canada in XXXX 2011, commenced attending a Christian church in order to manufacture a refugee claim: the claimant had photos taken of his church attendance and baptism in XXXX and XXXX 2011, and the church letter of August 2013 to bolster his fraudulent claim, coupled with his lack of basic knowledge of Christianity and the Bible, his inability to state the denomination of his church (although allegedly attending for 6 plus years) and his vague answers concerning major religious celebrations and what his religion did for him.
CONCLUSION

[14] Based on the totality of the evidence in this particular case, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee under s.96 nor a person in need of protection under s. 97 of the Act.

[15] The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
(signed)
"Diane L. Tinker"
Diane L. Tinker
February 6, 2018

2 Personal Information Form, Exhibit C-2.
3 C-7 Original Resident Identity Card, photocopy of the Hukou and Marriage Certificate, Exhibit M-1 photocopy of Chinese passport.
4 Exhibit C-7 photocopy of summons.
5 NDP for China s.9.3: Regulations on summonses and s.9.10 Samples of summonses and subpoenas.
6 Huang v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 288 at paras. 21-22.
7 Ibid., s.3.22 Fraudulent documents.
8 http://www.irb-cisr.gc.ca/Eng/BoaCom/references/pol/jurisprud/Pages/TB6-11632.aspx.
9 2017 FC 762.
10 TB6-11632 at paras. 25, 26, 29 and 31.

I find, on a balance of probabilities that the previous answers are vague and not from a person who has been a devout Christian for over eight years.

[13] In summary, I find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant, upon his arrival to Canada in XXXX 2011, commenced attending a Christian church in order to manufacture a refugee claim: the claimant had photos taken of his church attendance and baptism in XXXX and XXXX 2011, and the church letter of August 2013 to bolster his fraudulent claim, coupled with his lack of basic knowledge of Christianity and the Bible, his inability to state the denomination of his church (although allegedly attending for 6 plus years) and his vague answers concerning major religious celebrations and what his religion did for him.
CONCLUSION

[14] Based on the totality of the evidence in this particular case, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee under s.96 nor a person in need of protection under s. 97 of the Act.

[15] The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
(signed)
"Diane L. Tinker"

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX (the claimant) is a citizen of the People's Republic of China. The claimant claims to have well-founded fear of persecution at the hands of the Communist regime and in particular, the Public Security Bureau, by reason of his religion as a Christian under sections 96 and 97 of The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1
ALLEGATIONS

[2] The claimant alleges in his Personal Information Form2 that as a result of his wife having been forced to have an abortion, he became sad and despondent, he turned to an underground Christian church on the recommendation of a friend. The claimant maintains that he started to attend the underground Christian church in XXXX 2009. The claimant indicated that he attended regularly on Sundays. The claimant indicated that on XXXX XXXX, 2011, his underground Christian church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (the PSB). The claimant indicated that he was able to escape and went to the home of a relative. The claimant alleges that the PSB went to his home to arrest him for his underground Christian church activities. The claimant stated that arrangements were made with a snakehead (smuggler) to leave the country. The claimant came to Canada on or about XXXX XXXX, 2011, and claimed for refugee protection several days later.
DETERMINATION

[3] I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. I find that the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that on the balance of probabilities he would personally be subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to the People's Republic of China.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[4] The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documents filed3 establish his identity as a citizen of the People's Republic of China.
The claimant as a Member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China

[5] I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant stated that he went to the underground church every week and the second time he went to it (i.e. in XXXX 2009), he was given a Bible. The claimant was asked what he did at the underground church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant responded that there was a Bible reading. The claimant was asked if there was anything else. The claimant then said that the members would share their faith and when asked as to what that meant, he responded that members shared what they had learned from the Bible. When asked for a third time if there was anything else the claimant did at his underground Christian church, he indicated that members gave a donation and helped distribute flyers. The claimant was asked for a fourth time if there was anything else he did at his underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant responded that if a member faced hardship, then the other members would assist that person. The claimant was asked if praying was done at the underground church, to which he replied in the affirmative. When asked as to why he failed to mention prayers, the claimant stated that he was sorry and was nervous. I reject this explanation as prayers are a central aspect to any Christian church.

[6] The claimant was asked about the alleged raid by the PSB on his underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. The claimant indicated that when advised by the leader that the PSB were approaching, he ran out the back door. The claimant stated that he had to go across a frozen ditch, up a mountain with fruit trees to get to a public road. The claimant acknowledged that the PSB are the professional police force in the People's Republic of China. The claimant was asked if the PSB were going to raid this underground church, would they not have surrounded the building and not simply go to the front door so people could run out the back door. The claimant replied that the PSB could not get to the back door. When asked to explain, the claimant initially stated that there was only one way in and one way out. When asked again, the claimant stated that the road was one way so the PSB could not get to the back door. When asked if the PSB could go on foot to the back door, the claimant answered in the affirmative. The claimant was then asked if the PSB could get to the back door why was the house not surrounded, the claimant replied that the PSB did not know how to come to him and the others. I reject this explanation. If the PSB were going to raid this underground church, they would have surrounded the building and not simply go to the front door so people could run out the back door. Furthermore, the claimant would not have any knowledge as to what the PSB knew or did not know with regard to getting to the back door. The claimant was asked as to what he did upon escaping from the underground church. He replied that he went home. When it was pointed out to him that in his Personal Information Form, he stated that he went to the home of a distant cousin, the claimant then said it was his auntie's home and that his cousin lived there as well but that he always said that it was his home. I reject this explanation as I find that the claimant was simply trying to cover his mistake in his oral testimony.

[7] The claimant, to support his claim that he is wanted by the PSB filed a summons.4 The summons indicates that it is an "Arrest Summons". There is no objective evidence that the PSB issued an "arrest summons" as indicated in the National Documentation Package for China,5 dated October 31, 2017. Furthermore, as indicated in the decision of Huang v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), "overall credibility may affect the weight given to the documentary evidence".6 I am mindful of the presence of fraudulent documents7 from the People's Republic of China and since I have found that the claimant was not a member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China I therefore do not find that the summons proffered by the claimant to be authentic.
Exit from the People's Republic of China

[8] The claimant indicated that a snakehead (smuggler) was hired to assist him in leaving the People's Republic of China. When asked as to how he was able to leave the country if wanted by the PSB, the claimant responded that he did not know and that the smuggler had arranged everything. The claimant indicated that he used his genuine Chinese passport and showed it to a customs officer who stamped it. The claimant was asked if he had to show his passport to any other Chinese official to which he responded in the negative. I reject this explanation as the claimant would have had to have shown his passport to possibly more Chinese customs officials and at least to airline officials prior to boarding the plane.

[9] I have also considered the Chairperson's Jurisprudential Guide TB6-11632.8 I have also considered the opposing case law such as the recent decision in Huang v. MCI9 wherein Russell J. outlined case law and opposing arguments that must be considered when assessing a claimant's ability to leave the People's Republic of China on his or her own genuine passport. Among those arguments stated in the case law are the following key points: (a) That a well-placed bribe to an official with a computer may be sufficient to compromise the Golden Shield system, thereby permitting a claimant to leave the People's Republic of China undetected; and (b) Whereas corruption is endemic in the People's Republic of China, it is plausible for a snakehead (smuggler) may successfully help a claimant bypass the Golden Shield police computer system and authorities. I have reviewed TB6-11632 and find that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) did address and consider this opposing case law and these specific arguments.10 The RAD in TB6-11632 outlined extensive evidence in the national documentation package about exit controls in the People's Republic of China. Many of these exit controls were in place when the claimant left the country. I find that the claimant's description of his flight from the People's Republic of China is not consistent with that as described in the national documentation evidence. The claimant was quite vague with respect as to his ability to leave the People's Republic of China: he indicated that he showed his passport to only one Chinese official and then boarded a plane at the Beijing Airport. When asked as to how he avoided the Golden Shield computer system, the claimant indicated that he did not know. The national documentation evidence describes multiple levels of security checks and instances where passports are screened. I find that the claimant could not have successfully left the People's Republic of China in the manner he has described of showing his passport to one Chinese official who stamped, scanned or examined it and then was able to board a plane.

[10] I have also considered the opposing arguments regarding bribery and endemic corruption in the People's Republic of China. These arguments do not address my concerns in the current case as outlined in the previous paragraph. Where the claimant himself is not credible with respect to his travel through the airport, arguments about bribery and corruption make little difference. I adopt the reasoning of the RAD in TB6-11632. While it is plausible or possible that a wanted fugitive may be smuggled out of the People's Republic of China, I need not accept it or believe it to be probable in the current case. In the current case, given the claimant's lack of credibility about being a member of an underground Christian church, I find it unlikely that he was smuggled out of the country. I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not leave the People's Republic of China as he described using his own genuine Chinese passport. I therefore find that the claimant is not being sought by the Chinese authorities for being a member of an underground Christian church. In conclusion, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China and has never been wanted by Chinese authorities.
The Claimant as a Christian in Canada

[11] I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a Christian in Canada. The claimant had stated that he started to practice Christianity in the People's Republic of China in XXXX 2009 and also received a Bible within a couple of weeks of his first attendance. The claimant stated that he started attending the XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2011, and although he stated he was baptized in the People's Republic of China, was again baptized in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2011, as stated on his Baptism Certificate.11 The claimant stated that he had a Bible in Canada as of early May 2011 and one in the People's Republic of China as of November 2009, and read it in both countries. The claimant has twelve years of formal education. The claimant stated that he went to church here in Canada every week until the last few months because he hurt his back.

[12] The claimant was asked as to what the denomination of the XXXX XXXX XXXX and replied protestant. The claimant was asked again and was given examples such as Anglican, Methodist, and Presbyterian. The claimant indicated that he did not know. The claimant was asked to tell a story from the Old Testament, other than the story of creation. The claimant replied that he was nervous and could not remember. The claimant was asked to name the apostles. The claimant named some of the disciples. The claimant did know the concept of God existing in three persons, could provide limited information about Holy Communion: the cookie is the body of Christ and the grape juice the blood of Christ and did provide a parable from the New Testament. The claimant was asked about his activities at his church here in Canada. The claimant stated that basically he participated in activities at Christmas, Easter and Pentecost. When asked as to what these activities entailed, the claimant indicated that he went to church and prayed. I am mindful that the level of knowledge of one's professed religion is one that can reasonably be expected. The claimant alleges that he has been a Christian since November 2009, a period of over eight years and has been reading the Bible from that time as well. I find that the level of knowledge of Christianity of the claimant is extremely poor. He was not able to tell a story from the Old Testament (other than the story of creation) was not able to name the apostles and was extremely vague as to major religious celebrations such as Christmas and Easter at his church. Moreover, the Certificate of Baptism is from XXXX 2011, his photos12 are from XXXX 2011 and the church letter is dated August 20, 2013,13 indicating that if the claimant was truly a Christian and had been attending church here in Canada over six and a half years, would have more knowledge. Furthermore, when questioned by his counsel as what his religion does for him, the claimant replied that it changed his life and when asked to explain, stated that he feels lots of joy and when asked as to how his faith allows him so much joy, he indicated that after I read the Bible, he felt it. I find, on a balance of probabilities that the previous answers are vague and not from a person who has been a devout Christian for over eight years.

[13] In summary, I find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant, upon his arrival to Canada in XXXX 2011, commenced attending a Christian church in order to manufacture a refugee claim: the claimant had photos taken of his church attendance and baptism in XXXX and XXXX 2011, and the church letter of August 2013 to bolster his fraudulent claim, coupled with his lack of basic knowledge of Christianity and the Bible, his inability to state the denomination of his church (although allegedly attending for 6 plus years) and his vague answers concerning major religious celebrations and what his religion did for him.
CONCLUSION
[14] Based on the totality of the evidence in this particular case, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee under s.96 nor a person in need of protection under s. 97 of the Act.

[15] The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
(signed)
"Diane L. Tinker"
